Hi, Aguinaldo. I have ten minutes before my next call. How did the meeting with the agency go?
It went well. The director confirmed that the new rule would be published in May.
That is good news. Did he say anything about the transition period?
Yes. He said it would be twelve months. But he warned us that the penalties could be higher than in the draft.
Higher? Our client will not like that. Did anybody ask why?
I did. He told us they had received many complaints about safety. And off the record, he said the minister wanted a stronger rule.
Okay. Can you put that in writing for the client, without the off-the-record part?
Of course. I will send a short debrief this afternoon, with only what was said in the official statement.

Every time one of my associates comes back from a meeting, I ask for a debrief, and I always give the same instructions. One page, or five sentences in an email. Start with what was decided or confirmed. Then what the other side warned us about. Then what they asked us to do. Use the right verb. If the regulator only suggested something, don't write that he confirmed it. That is how clients make bad decisions. And one more rule: anything that was said off the record never goes in writing. You can tell me on the phone, but you never write it.

A few years ago, I received a report after a meeting with the energy agency. It said the agency had approved our new tariff. So we told the banks, and we told the press. Two weeks later, we discovered the truth. The director had said the agency would probably approve the tariff, but only after the public consultation. Probably. After the consultation. Those two small details changed everything, and we had to publish a correction. Since then, I ask for the same thing in every report: the exact words, or at least the exact verb. Did they confirm it, or did they only suggest it?

The minister of infrastructure said yesterday that the new concession program would attract fifty billion dollars in private investment over the next four years. Speaking at a conference in São Paulo, she told investors that the first tenders would open in March. She acknowledged that some concessions had been delayed in the past, but she stated that the new rules were simpler. In a statement published later, the national investors' association welcomed the program, but it warned that the rules had to be clear before the tenders. It also recommended a longer public consultation.
